shared.concept_anchor: Regulating Act 1773 Supreme Court Calcutta

en.display_text:
Which of the following statements correctly describes a key feature of the Regulating Act 1773?

(a) It established a High Court at Calcutta to exercise jurisdiction over all inhabitants of Bengal
(b) The Supreme Court established by this Act had universal jurisdiction over all residents of Bengal, including the Governor-General
(c) It subordinated the Presidencies of Bombay and Madras to the Governor-General in Council at Calcutta in matters of war and diplomacy
(d) Warren Hastings was appointed as the first President of the Board of Control under this Act
en.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because students associate the 1773 Act primarily with the Governor-General position and may assume the Supreme Court was established by a separate, later legislation.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): the Regulating Act 1773 itself established the Supreme Court at Calcutta — it was not a separate High Court established later.
Eliminate option (b): the Supreme Court at Calcutta had jurisdiction over British subjects, not all inhabitants of Bengal, creating a famous conflict with the Council.
Eliminate option (d): Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General under the Regulating Act 1773, not the President of the Board of Control — that body came with Pitt's India Act 1784.
Option (c) is correct: the Regulating Act 1773 subordinated the Presidencies of Bombay and Madras to the Governor-General in Council at Calcutta for matters of war and peace.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Students often conflate the Supreme Court established under the Regulating Act 1773 with the High Courts established under the High Courts Act 1861. The plausible-fabrication trap here is option (b), which inverts the actual jurisdictional scope — the Supreme Court's jurisdiction over 'all inhabitants' was precisely what caused its conflict with the Governor-General's Council, since the Council itself was theoretically subject to the Court's jurisdiction, a constitutional anomaly that plagued administration for years.
en.final_explanation:
The Regulating Act 1773 was the first step by the British Parliament to regulate the East India Company's affairs in India. It created the position of Governor-General of Bengal and established a Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774) — the first such court in India.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Supreme Court at Calcutta was established by the Regulating Act 1773 itself, not by a subsequent separate enactment.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The Court's jurisdiction extended over British subjects and the Company's servants, not uniformly over all inhabitants — this ambiguity caused severe administrative conflicts.
• Option (c) — Correct: The Presidencies of Bombay and Madras were subordinated to the Governor-General in Council at Calcutta in matters of war, peace, and diplomacy.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Warren Hastings became the first Governor-General; the Board of Control was a creation of Pitt's India Act 1784, not the 1773 Act.

Value Addition:
• The first Governor-General under the 1773 Act was Warren Hastings; he faced impeachment proceedings later.
• The Supreme Court at Calcutta comprised a Chief Justice and three puisne judges.
• The jurisdictional conflict between the Supreme Court and the Council was partially resolved only through the Amending Act of 1781.

hi.display_text:
रेगुलेटिंग एक्ट 1773 की निम्नलिखित में से कौन-सी विशेषता सही रूप से वर्णित करती है?

(a) इसने कोलकाता में एक उच्च न्यायालय की स्थापना की जो बंगाल के सभी निवासियों पर अधिकार करता था
(b) इस अधिनियम द्वारा स्थापित सुप्रीम कोर्ट का बंगाल के सभी निवासियों, जिसमें गवर्नर-जनरल भी शामिल हैं, पर सार्वभौमिक अधिकार क्षेत्र था
(c) इसने बॉम्बे और मद्रास के प्रेसिडेंसी को युद्ध और कूटनीति के मामलों में कोलकाता में गवर्नर-जनरल इन काउंसिल के अधीन कर दिया
(d) वॉरेन हेस्टिंग्स को इस अधिनियम के तहत बोर्ड ऑफ कंट्रोल का पहला अध्यक्ष नियुक्त किया गया
hi.strong_distractor: a — विकल्प a भ्रामक है क्योंकि छात्र 1773 के अधिनियम को मुख्य रूप से गवर्नर-जनरल पद से जोड़ते हैं और मान सकते हैं कि सुप्रीम कोर्ट किसी अलग, बाद के कानून द्वारा स्थापित किया गया था।
elimination_logic: विकल्प (a) को खारिज करें: रेगुलेटिंग एक्ट 1773 ने स्वयं कोलकाता में सुप्रीम कोर्ट की स्थापना की — यह कोई अलग उच्च न्यायालय नहीं था जो बाद में स्थापित किया गया हो।
विकल्प (b) को खारिज करें: कोलकाता का सुप्रीम कोर्ट केवल ब्रिटिश नागरिकों पर अधिकार रखता था, बंगाल के सभी निवासियों पर नहीं, जिससे परिषद के साथ एक प्रसिद्ध विवाद उत्पन्न हुआ।
विकल्प (d) को खारिज करें: वॉरेन हेस्टिंग्स रेगुलेटिंग एक्ट 1773 के तहत पहले गवर्नर-जनरल थे, बोर्ड ऑफ कंट्रोल के अध्यक्ष नहीं — वह संस्था पिट के इंडिया एक्ट 1784 के साथ आई।
विकल्प (c) सही है: रेगुलेटिंग एक्ट 1773 ने बॉम्बे और मद्रास के प्रेसिडेंसी को युद्ध और शांति के मामलों में कोलकाता में गवर्नर-जनरल इन काउंसिल के अधीन कर दिया।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: छात्र अक्सर रेगुलेटिंग एक्ट 1773 के तहत स्थापित सुप्रीम कोर्ट को हाई कोर्ट्स एक्ट 1861 के तहत स्थापित उच्च न्यायालयों से भ्रमित कर देते हैं। यहां संभावित भ्रांति का जाल विकल्प (b) है, जो वास्तविक अधिकार क्षेत्र को उलट देता है — सुप्रीम कोर्ट का 'सभी निवासियों' पर अधिकार क्षेत्र ही वह कारण था जिसने गवर्नर-जनरल की परिषद के साथ उसका विवाद उत्पन्न किया, क्योंकि परिषद स्वयं सैद्धांतिक रूप से कोर्ट के अधिकार क्षेत्र के अधीन थी, जो प्रशासन के लिए वर्षों तक संवैधानिक समस्या बनी रही।
hi.final_explanation:
रेगुलेटिंग एक्ट 1773 ब्रिटिश संसद द्वारा भारत में ईस्ट इंडिया कंपनी के मामलों को नियंत्रित करने का पहला कदम था। इसने बंगाल के गवर्नर-जनरल का पद स्थापित किया और कोलकाता में सुप्रीम कोर्ट (1774) की स्थापना की — भारत में ऐसा पहला न्यायालय।

• विकल्प (a) — गलत: कोलकाता का सुप्रीम कोर्ट रेगुलेटिंग एक्ट 1773 द्वारा स्थापित था, किसी बाद के अलग कानून द्वारा नहीं।
• विकल्प (b) — गलत: कोर्ट का अधिकार क्षेत्र ब्रिटिश नागरिकों और कंपनी के कर्मचारियों तक सीमित था, सभी निवासियों पर समान रूप से नहीं — इस अस्पष्टता ने प्रशासनिक विवाद उत्पन्न किए।
• विकल्प (c) — सही: बॉम्बे और मद्रास के प्रेसिडेंसी को युद्ध, शांति और कूटनीति के मामलों में कोलकाता में गवर्नर-जनरल इन काउंसिल के अधीन कर दिया गया।
• विकल्प (d) — गलत: वॉरेन हेस्टिंग्स पहले गवर्नर-जनरल बने; बोर्ड ऑफ कंट्रोल पिट के इंडिया एक्ट 1784 की रचना थी, 1773 के अधिनियम की नहीं।

Value Addition:
• 1773 के अधिनियम के तहत पहला गवर्नर-जनरल वॉरेन हेस्टिंग्स था; बाद में उन पर महाभियोग चलाया गया।
• कोलकाता के सुप्रीम कोर्ट में एक मुख्य न्यायाधीश और तीन अन्य न्यायाधीश थे।
• सुप्रीम कोर्ट और परिषद के बीच अधिकार क्षेत्र का विवाद आंशिक रूप से 1781 के संशोधन अधिनियम के माध्यम से ही सुलझा।

shared.concept_anchor: Pitt's India Act 1784 dual government Board of Control

en.display_text:
With reference to Pitt's India Act 1784, consider the following statements:

1. The Board of Control established under this Act had authority over both the commercial and political affairs of the East India Company.
2. This Act marked the beginning of direct British Government control over Indian political administration.
3. The Governor-General was granted emergency override powers, allowing action without Council concurrence in urgent situations.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

(a) 1 and 2 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 1 and 3 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3

statement_analysis.statement: The Board of Control established under Pitt's India Act 1784 had authority over both commercial and political affairs of the East India Company.
statement_analysis.reason: The Board of Control's jurisdiction was explicitly confined to political, military, and revenue affairs; commercial affairs remained exclusively with the Court of Directors.

statement_analysis.statement: Pitt's India Act 1784 marked the beginning of direct British Government control over Indian administration.
statement_analysis.reason: Through the Board of Control, the British Crown for the first time exercised supervisory authority over the Company's political and administrative decisions, earning the Act recognition as the beginning of Crown paramountcy.

statement_analysis.statement: The Governor-General was granted emergency override powers under Pitt's India Act 1784, allowing him to act without Council concurrence in urgent situations.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act significantly enhanced the Governor-General's powers, including provisions that allowed him to override his Council in military emergencies.

en.strong_distractor: d — Option d (1 only) is deceptive because students aware of the Board of Control's role may broadly assume it controlled all Company functions, making Statement 1 appear correct and Statements 2 and 3 appear redundant.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The Board of Control handled political/military/revenue affairs; commercial affairs stayed with the Court of Directors — Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: Pitt's India Act is explicitly recognised as the beginning of British Government's direct control over Indian political administration — Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: The Act gave the Governor-General enhanced emergency powers to act without Council — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct, pointing to option (b).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the scope-extension trap: students know the Board of Control was powerful and may assume its remit covered all Company functions. The precise fact — that commercial affairs were kept separate under the Court of Directors — is often glossed over. A partially prepared student selects option (d) believing Statement 1 is also correct, missing the demarcation central to the 'dual government' concept.
en.final_explanation:
Pitt's India Act 1784 created the famous dual government system for India: the Court of Directors retained control over commercial affairs while a newly created Board of Control, comprising Crown-appointed members including a Secretary of State and the Chancellor of the Exchequer, supervised all political, military, and revenue matters.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Board of Control's jurisdiction was confined to political, military, and revenue affairs. Commercial activities of the Company remained exclusively with the Court of Directors — this separation was the essence of the 'dual' system.
• Statement 2 — Correct: This Act is textbook-recognised as the starting point of direct British Government supervision over Indian governance, predating formal Crown rule by over seven decades.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Governor-General received enhanced powers, including emergency override provisions, making the position far more authoritative than under the Regulating Act 1773.

Value Addition:
• William Pitt the Younger introduced this Act; it gave Parliament its first real grip over Company governance.
• The Act declared the policy of 'non-interference' with Indian territories — though it was rarely followed.
• The dual government lasted until the Government of India Act 1858 abolished both the Board of Control and the Court of Directors.

hi.display_text:
पिट्स इंडिया एक्ट 1784 के संदर्भ में, निम्नलिखित कथनों पर विचार करें:

1. इस अधिनियम के तहत स्थापित Board of Control को ईस्ट इंडिया कंपनी के वाणिज्यिक और राजनीतिक दोनों मामलों पर अधिकार था।
2. इस अधिनियम ने भारतीय राजनीतिक प्रशासन पर ब्रिटिश सरकार के प्रत्यक्ष नियंत्रण की शुरुआत की।
3. गवर्नर-जनरल को आपातकालीन ओवरराइड अधिकार दिए गए, जिससे वह आवश्यक स्थिति में परिषद की सहमति के बिना कार्य कर सकता था।

उपरोक्त में से कौन-सा/से कथन सही है/हैं?

(a) केवल 1 और 2
(b) केवल 2 और 3
(c) केवल 1 और 3
(d) 1, 2 और 3

statement_analysis.statement: The Board of Control established under Pitt's India Act 1784 had authority over both commercial and political affairs of the East India Company.
statement_analysis.reason: Board of Control का अधिकार क्षेत्र स्पष्ट रूप से राजनीतिक, सैन्य और राजस्व मामलों तक सीमित था; वाणिज्यिक मामले पूरी तरह से Court of Directors के अधीन थे।

statement_analysis.statement: Pitt's India Act 1784 marked the beginning of direct British Government control over Indian administration.
statement_analysis.reason: Board of Control के माध्यम से, ब्रिटिश क्राउन ने पहली बार कंपनी के राजनीतिक और प्रशासनिक निर्णयों पर पर्यवेक्षण अधिकार का प्रयोग किया, जिससे इस अधिनियम को क्राउन की सर्वोच्चता की शुरुआत माना जाता है।

statement_analysis.statement: The Governor-General was granted emergency override powers under Pitt's India Act 1784, allowing him to act without Council concurrence in urgent situations.
statement_analysis.reason: इस अधिनियम ने गवर्नर-जनरल के अधिकारों को काफी बढ़ाया, जिसमें सैन्य आपात स्थितियों में परिषद की सहमति के बिना कार्य करने की शक्ति भी शामिल थी।

hi.strong_distractor: d — विकल्प d (केवल 1) भ्रामक है क्योंकि बोर्ड ऑफ कंट्रोल की भूमिका से परिचित छात्र सामान्यतः मान लेते हैं कि यह कंपनी के सभी कार्यों को नियंत्रित करता था, जिससे कथन 1 सही प्रतीत होता है और कथन 2 और 3 अनावश्यक लगते हैं।
elimination_logic: कथन 1 का मूल्यांकन करें: बोर्ड ऑफ कंट्रोल राजनीतिक/सैन्य/राजस्व मामलों को संभालता था; वाणिज्यिक मामले Court of Directors के पास थे — अतः कथन 1 गलत है।
कथन 2 का मूल्यांकन करें: पिट्स इंडिया एक्ट को स्पष्ट रूप से भारतीय राजनीतिक प्रशासन पर ब्रिटिश सरकार के प्रत्यक्ष नियंत्रण की शुरुआत माना जाता है — अतः कथन 2 सही है।
कथन 3 का मूल्यांकन करें: इस अधिनियम ने गवर्नर-जनरल को परिषद की सहमति के बिना आपातकालीन कार्यवाही करने के लिए अधिकार दिए — अतः कथन 3 सही है।
केवल कथन 2 और 3 सही हैं, जो विकल्प (b) की ओर संकेत करते हैं।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: कथन 1 में स्कोप-एक्सटेंशन ट्रैप का उपयोग किया गया है: छात्र जानते हैं कि बोर्ड ऑफ कंट्रोल शक्तिशाली था और मान लेते हैं कि इसका अधिकार कंपनी के सभी कार्यों पर था। वास्तविक तथ्य — कि वाणिज्यिक मामले Court of Directors के अधीन थे — अक्सर अनदेखा कर दिया जाता है। आंशिक रूप से तैयार छात्र विकल्प (d) चुनते हैं यह सोचकर कि कथन 1 भी सही है, जिससे 'डुअल गवर्नमेंट' अवधारणा की केंद्रीय सीमा छूट जाती है।
hi.final_explanation:
पिट्स इंडिया एक्ट 1784 ने भारत के लिए प्रसिद्ध द्वैध शासन प्रणाली बनाई: Court of Directors ने वाणिज्यिक मामलों का नियंत्रण रखा जबकि एक नया Board of Control, जिसमें क्राउन द्वारा नियुक्त सदस्य जैसे सचिव और चांसलर ऑफ़ एक्सचेकर शामिल थे, ने सभी राजनीतिक, सैन्य और राजस्व मामलों की निगरानी की।

• कथन 1 — गलत: Board of Control का अधिकार क्षेत्र केवल राजनीतिक, सैन्य और राजस्व मामलों तक सीमित था। कंपनी की वाणिज्यिक गतिविधियाँ पूरी तरह से Court of Directors के अधीन थीं — यही 'डुअल' प्रणाली का सार था।
• कथन 2 — सही: यह अधिनियम भारतीय शासन पर ब्रिटिश सरकार के प्रत्यक्ष पर्यवेक्षण की शुरुआत के रूप में मान्यता प्राप्त है, जो औपचारिक क्राउन शासन से सात दशकों से अधिक पहले था।
• कथन 3 — सही: गवर्नर-जनरल को बढ़ाए गए अधिकार मिले, जिनमें आपातकालीन ओवरराइड प्रावधान शामिल थे, जिससे यह पद रेगुलेटिंग एक्ट 1773 की तुलना में अधिक शक्तिशाली हो गया।

Value Addition:
• विलियम पिट द यंगर ने यह अधिनियम पेश किया; इसने संसद को कंपनी शासन पर पहला वास्तविक नियंत्रण दिया।
• इस अधिनियम ने भारतीय क्षेत्रों में 'गैर-हस्तक्षेप' की नीति घोषित की — हालांकि इसे शायद ही कभी लागू किया गया।
• द्वैध शासन तब तक चला जब तक कि भारत सरकार अधिनियम 1858 ने Board of Control और Court of Directors दोनों को समाप्त नहीं कर दिया।

en.display_text:
Consider the following statements about the Charter Act 1853:

1. It introduced competitive examinations for entry into the Civil Services of the East India Company.
2. It fixed the renewal period of the Company's charter at twenty years, similar to previous Charter Acts.
3. It separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council by creating a distinct Legislative Council.
4. The Legislative Council created under this Act included members nominated by provincial governments, giving it a representative character.

How many of the above statements are correct?

(a) Only one
(b) Only two
(c) Only three
(d) All four

statement_analysis.statement: The Charter Act 1853 introduced competitive examinations for entry into the Civil Services of the East India Company.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1853 Act replaced patronage-based appointment with open competitive examination, acting on the Macaulay Committee's recommendations.

statement_analysis.statement: The Charter Act 1853 fixed the renewal period of the Company's charter at twenty years, similar to previous Charter Acts.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike previous Charter Acts of 1793, 1813, and 1833 (which had fixed 20-year renewal periods), the 1853 Act did not specify any time limit for the Company's charter — its continuation was left open-ended.

statement_analysis.statement: The 1853 Act separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council by creating a distinct Legislative Council.
statement_analysis.reason: Six new members were added to the Governor-General's Council for legislative purposes, effectively creating a mini-legislature distinct from the executive Council.

statement_analysis.statement: The Legislative Council created under the 1853 Act included members nominated by provincial governments, giving it a representative character.
statement_analysis.reason: The six additional legislative councillors included representatives nominated by the local governments of Bengal, Bombay, Madras, and the North-Western Provinces — giving the Council a nascent representative character.

en.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Only two) is deceptive because Statement 2 contains a plausible claim — students often assume all Charter Acts followed a standard 20-year renewal cycle, making this error easy to miss.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Competitive examinations for civil services were introduced by the 1853 Act — Correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Previous Charter Acts had 20-year limits, but the 1853 Act had no fixed renewal period — this is a signature feature of 1853; Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: The separation of legislative and executive functions in the Council is a textbook feature of 1853 — Correct.
Evaluate Statement 4: Provincial government nominations to the Legislative Council gave it representative character — Correct.
Three statements (1, 3, 4) are correct, pointing to option (c) — 'Only three'.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits students' tendency to apply a uniform pattern to Charter Acts — all prior Acts (1793, 1813, 1833) carried 20-year renewable charters. The 1853 Act is uniquely distinguished by removing this time limit entirely, signalling Parliament's uncertainty about the Company's future. A partially prepared student, recalling the 20-year pattern, marks Statement 2 as correct and underestimates the total to 'Only two,' selecting option (b).
en.final_explanation:
The Charter Act 1853 was the last Charter Act and functioned almost as a transitional document. It introduced several innovations while also signalling the impending end of Company rule.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Open competitive examination replaced the system of patronage for civil service recruitment, a revolutionary change driven by the Macaulay Committee report.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Unlike the 1793, 1813, and 1833 Acts, the 1853 Act contained no fixed time limit for the Company's rule — Parliament deliberately kept the future open.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Six additional members were added to the Council exclusively for legislative business, separating legislative from executive functions for the first time.
• Statement 4 — Correct: The additional members were nominated by the local governments of Bengal, Bombay, Madras, and NWFP, giving the body a representative texture.

Value Addition:
• The 1853 Legislative Council has been called the 'forerunner of the Indian Parliament.'
• The competitive examination introduced in 1853 was held in London only, effectively excluding most Indians until the age limit was raised later.
• The 1858 Act abolished Company rule just five years after this Act — making 1853 the last of the Company-era Charter Acts.

hi.upsc_trap_explanation: कथन 2 छात्रों की चार्टर अधिनियमों पर एक समान पैटर्न लागू करने की प्रवृत्ति का लाभ उठाता है — सभी पूर्व के अधिनियम (1793, 1813, 1833) में 20 वर्ष की नवीनीकरण अवधि थी। 1853 का अधिनियम इस समय सीमा को पूरी तरह हटा देता है, जो संसद की कंपनी के भविष्य को लेकर अनिश्चितता को दर्शाता है। आंशिक रूप से तैयार छात्र 20 वर्ष के पैटर्न को याद करके कथन 2 को सही मान लेते हैं और कुल सही कथनों को 'केवल दो' समझकर विकल्प (b) चुन लेते हैं।
hi.final_explanation:
चार्टर अधिनियम 1853 अंतिम चार्टर अधिनियम था और लगभग एक संक्रमणकालीन दस्तावेज के रूप में कार्य करता था। इसने कई नवाचार प्रस्तुत किए और कंपनी शासन के अंत का संकेत भी दिया।

• कथन 1 — सही: सिविल सेवा भर्ती के लिए संरक्षण प्रणाली की जगह खुली प्रतियोगी परीक्षा प्रणाली लाई गई, जो मैकाले समिति की रिपोर्ट द्वारा प्रेरित एक क्रांतिकारी बदलाव था।
• कथन 2 — गलत: 1793, 1813 और 1833 के अधिनियमों के विपरीत, 1853 के अधिनियम में कंपनी शासन के लिए कोई निश्चित समय सीमा नहीं थी — संसद ने जानबूझकर भविष्य को खुला रखा।
• कथन 3 — सही: परिषद में केवल विधायी कार्यों के लिए छह अतिरिक्त सदस्य जोड़े गए, जिससे पहली बार विधायी और कार्यकारी कार्यों का पृथक्करण हुआ।
• कथन 4 — सही: अतिरिक्त सदस्यों को बंगाल, बॉम्बे, मद्रास और उत्तर-पश्चिमी प्रांतों की स्थानीय सरकारों द्वारा नामित किया गया, जिससे परिषद को प्रतिनिधित्वात्मक स्वरूप मिला।

Value Addition:
• 1853 की विधायी परिषद को 'भारतीय संसद का पूर्ववर्ती' कहा गया है।
• 1853 में शुरू की गई प्रतियोगी परीक्षा केवल लंदन में आयोजित होती थी, जिससे अधिकांश भारतीयों को उम्र सीमा बढ़ाए जाने तक प्रभावी रूप से बाहर रखा गया।
• 1858 का अधिनियम कंपनी शासन को केवल पांच वर्ष बाद समाप्त कर देता है — जिससे 1853 कंपनी युग के चार्टर अधिनियमों का अंतिम अधिनियम बन जाता है।

en.strong_distractor: c — Option c swaps the Council of India's advisory role with the Secretary of State's direct authority, a confusion many students have about which body held real power after 1858.
elimination_logic: Identify unambiguous pairs first: The Board of Control was abolished by the 1858 Act (A-3) — this is a textbook fact.
The Secretary of State for India was created by the 1858 Act with a Council of India (B-1) — confirmed.
The Governor-General becoming Viceroy is a direct feature of 1858 (C-4) — confirmed.
The Court of Directors was the Company's own governing body that was abolished in 1858, not merged into any Crown body (D-2) — confirmed; option (b) is correct.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap targets students who confuse the 'Court of Directors' with the 'Council of India.' After 1858, the Court of Directors was abolished entirely, while the Council of India was a new body advising the Secretary of State. Students who recall that 'both Company bodies were replaced' may incorrectly pair the Court of Directors with the Secretary of State's powers rather than correctly identifying its abolition.
en.final_explanation:
The Government of India Act 1858 ended Company rule and transferred governance to the British Crown. It abolished the dual government structure created by Pitt's India Act 1784.

Correct pairings:
• A (Board of Control) — 3 (Abolished by the 1858 Act): The Board of Control, created under Pitt's India Act 1784, was dissolved. Its functions passed to the Secretary of State.
• B (Secretary of State for India) — 1 (Assisted by a 15-member Council of India): The Secretary of State, a Cabinet member, was supported by a 15-member advisory Council of India composed largely of retired India hands.
• C (Governor-General) — 4 (Became Viceroy, representing the Crown directly): Lord Canning became the first Viceroy. The title 'Viceroy' reflected his dual capacity — Governor-General for domestic affairs and direct Crown representative.
• D (Court of Directors) — 2 (Abolished; its patronage powers extinguished): The Court of Directors, the Company's own elected governing board, was abolished outright — ending the era of Company self-governance.

Value Addition:
• Lord Canning was simultaneously the last Governor-General and the first Viceroy.
• The Council of India had 15 members; at least 9 had to have served in India for at least 10 years.
• The 1858 Act is sometimes called the 'Act for the Better Government of India.'

elimination_logic: स्पष्ट जोड़ों की पहचान पहले करें: बोर्ड ऑफ कंट्रोल को 1858 के अधिनियम द्वारा समाप्त किया गया था (A-3) — यह एक पाठ्यपुस्तक तथ्य है।
सेक्रेटरी ऑफ स्टेट फॉर इंडिया को 1858 के अधिनियम द्वारा काउंसिल ऑफ इंडिया के साथ बनाया गया था (B-1) — पुष्टि हुई।
गवर्नर-जनरल का वाइसराय बनना 1858 की एक सीधी विशेषता है (C-4) — पुष्टि हुई।
कोर्ट ऑफ डायरेक्टर्स कंपनी की अपनी शासी संस्था थी जिसे 1858 में समाप्त किया गया, किसी क्राउन निकाय में विलय नहीं किया गया (D-2) — पुष्टि हुई; विकल्प (b) सही है।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: एंटिटी-स्वैप जाल उन छात्रों को लक्षित करता है जो 'कोर्ट ऑफ डायरेक्टर्स' को 'काउंसिल ऑफ इंडिया' के साथ भ्रमित करते हैं। 1858 के बाद, कोर्ट ऑफ डायरेक्टर्स पूरी तरह से समाप्त कर दिया गया था, जबकि काउंसिल ऑफ इंडिया सेक्रेटरी ऑफ स्टेट की सलाह देने वाली नई संस्था थी। जो छात्र याद करते हैं कि 'दोनों कंपनी निकायों को प्रतिस्थापित किया गया' था, वे गलत तरीके से कोर्ट ऑफ डायरेक्टर्स को सेक्रेटरी ऑफ स्टेट के अधिकारों के साथ जोड़ सकते हैं बजाय इसके कि वे इसकी समाप्ति को सही ढंग से पहचानें।
hi.final_explanation:
भारत सरकार अधिनियम 1858 ने कंपनी शासन को समाप्त कर ब्रिटिश क्राउन को शासन सौंप दिया। इसने पिट्ट के भारत अधिनियम 1784 द्वारा बनाए गए द्वैध शासन ढांचे को समाप्त किया।

सही जोड़े:
• A (बोर्ड ऑफ कंट्रोल) — 3 (1858 के अधिनियम द्वारा समाप्त): बोर्ड ऑफ कंट्रोल, जो पिट्ट के भारत अधिनियम 1784 के तहत बनाया गया था, को भंग कर दिया गया। इसके कार्य सेक्रेटरी ऑफ स्टेट को सौंपे गए।
• B (सेक्रेटरी ऑफ स्टेट फॉर इंडिया) — 1 (15-सदस्यीय काउंसिल ऑफ इंडिया द्वारा सहायता प्राप्त): सेक्रेटरी ऑफ स्टेट, जो कैबिनेट सदस्य था, को 15-सदस्यीय सलाहकार काउंसिल ऑफ इंडिया द्वारा सहायता मिली, जिसमें अधिकांश सेवानिवृत्त भारत के अधिकारी थे।
• C (गवर्नर-जनरल) — 4 (वाइसराय बना, जो सीधे क्राउन का प्रतिनिधित्व करता था): लॉर्ड कैनिंग पहले वाइसराय बने। 'वाइसराय' की उपाधि उनके दोहरे पद को दर्शाती थी — घरेलू मामलों के लिए गवर्नर-जनरल और सीधे क्राउन के प्रतिनिधि।
• D (कोर्ट ऑफ डायरेक्टर्स) — 2 (समाप्त; इसके संरक्षक अधिकार समाप्त): कोर्ट ऑफ डायरेक्टर्स, कंपनी की अपनी निर्वाचित शासी परिषद, को पूरी तरह समाप्त कर दिया गया — कंपनी के स्व-शासन का युग समाप्त।

Value Addition:
• लॉर्ड कैनिंग एक साथ अंतिम गवर्नर-जनरल और पहले वाइसराय थे।
• काउंसिल ऑफ इंडिया में 15 सदस्य थे; कम से कम 9 को भारत में कम से कम 10 वर्ष सेवा करनी आवश्यक थी।

en.display_text:
Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence in the evolution of the electoral principle in Indian Legislative Councils?

1. Introduction of indirect election through bodies such as universities and chambers of commerce
2. Pure nomination of non-official members with no electoral element
3. Introduction of direct elections for the first time
4. Extension of direct elections with dyarchy and expanded franchise

(a) 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
(b) 2 → 1 → 4 → 3
(c) 2 → 1 → 3 → 4
(d) 4 → 3 → 1 → 2
en.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because students who know the 1892 Act introduced some form of electoral principle may incorrectly place the 1909 Act's 'direct election' before the 1892 indirect nomination step.
elimination_logic: Fix anchor points: The Indian Councils Act 1861 was purely nominative — no electoral element — and comes first.
The Indian Councils Act 1892 introduced indirect electoral principle (through bodies like universities and chambers of commerce) — second.
The Indian Councils Act 1909 introduced direct elections for the first time — third; the 1919 Act expanded this further.
Correct sequence: 1861 → 1892 → 1909 → 1919, which corresponds to option (c).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap works here because students may conflate the 1892 Act's 'indirect nomination through electoral colleges' with the 1909 Act's 'direct elections,' reversing their positions. Additionally, those who do not remember that the 1861 Act was the baseline of pure nomination may place it after 1892.
en.final_explanation:
This chronology tracks the evolution of the electoral principle in Indian legislative councils.

Correct sequence — 1861 → 1892 → 1909 → 1919:
• 1861: Indian Councils Act introduced non-official members to the Legislative Council, but purely through nomination — no electoral element whatsoever.
• 1892: Indian Councils Act introduced the indirect election principle (the term 'election' was deliberately avoided). Bodies such as universities, district boards, municipalities, and chambers of commerce recommended names from which the Governor-General nominated members.
• 1909: Indian Councils Act (Morley-Minto Reforms) introduced direct elections for the first time in Indian legislative history, alongside the controversial separate Muslim electorate.
• 1919: Government of India Act expanded the electorate further and introduced dyarchy, extending voting rights based on property/educational qualifications.

Why wrong options fail:
• Option (a) reverses 1892 and 1909.
• Option (b) places 1919 before 1909.
• Option (d) inverts the entire sequence.

Value Addition:
• The 1892 Act is described as introducing elections 'in principle' without using the word.
• The 1909 Act created the first elected non-official majority in provincial councils.
• The Montagu-Chelmsford Report of 1918 directly preceded the 1919 Act.

भारतीय विधान परिषदों में चुनावी सिद्धांत के विकास में निम्नलिखित में से कौन-सा सही कालानुक्रमिक क्रम दर्शाता है?

3. पहली बार प्रत्यक्ष चुनाव की शुरुआत
4. द्विध्रुवीय शासन और विस्तारित मताधिकार के साथ प्रत्यक्ष चुनाव का विस्तार

(a) 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
(b) 2 → 1 → 4 → 3
(c) 2 → 1 → 3 → 4
(d) 4 → 3 → 1 → 2
hi.strong_distractor: b — विकल्प b भ्रमित करने वाला है क्योंकि जो छात्र जानते हैं कि 1892 के अधिनियम ने किसी न किसी रूप में चुनावी सिद्धांत पेश किया था, वे 1909 के अधिनियम के 'प्रत्यक्ष चुनाव' को 1892 के अप्रत्यक्ष नामांकन से पहले गलत तरीके से रख सकते हैं।
elimination_logic: एंकर पॉइंट तय करें: Indian Councils Act 1861 पूरी तरह से नामांकन आधारित था — कोई चुनावी तत्व नहीं था — और यह सबसे पहला है।
Indian Councils Act 1892 ने अप्रत्यक्ष चुनावी सिद्धांत पेश किया (जैसे विश्वविद्यालयों और वाणिज्य मंडलों के माध्यम से) — दूसरा।

hi.upsc_trap_explanation: यह temporal-swap जाल इसलिए काम करता है क्योंकि छात्र 1892 के अधिनियम के 'चुनावी कॉलेजों के माध्यम से अप्रत्यक्ष नामांकन' को 1909 के 'प्रत्यक्ष चुनाव' के साथ भ्रमित कर सकते हैं, और उनकी स्थिति उलट सकते हैं। इसके अतिरिक्त, जो छात्र याद नहीं रखते कि 1861 का अधिनियम पूरी तरह नामांकन आधारित था, वे इसे 1892 के बाद रख सकते हैं।

सही क्रम — 1861 → 1892 → 1909 → 1919:
• 1861: Indian Councils Act ने विधान परिषद में गैर-आधिकारिक सदस्यों को नामांकित किया, लेकिन पूरी तरह नामांकन के माध्यम से — कोई चुनावी तत्व नहीं।
• 1892: Indian Councils Act ने अप्रत्यक्ष चुनावी सिद्धांत पेश किया (शब्द 'चुनाव' जानबूझकर टाला गया)। विश्वविद्यालय, जिला बोर्ड, नगरपालिका, और वाणिज्य मंडल जैसे निकायों ने नाम सुझाए, जिनमें से गवर्नर-जनरल ने सदस्यों का नामांकन किया।
• 1909: Indian Councils Act (Morley-Minto सुधार) ने पहली बार भारतीय विधान इतिहास में प्रत्यक्ष चुनाव पेश किया, साथ ही विवादास्पद अलग मुस्लिम मतदाता मंडल भी।
• 1919: Government of India Act ने मतदाता संख्या बढ़ाई और द्विध्रुवीय शासन (dyarchy) पेश किया, संपत्ति/शैक्षिक योग्यता के आधार पर मतदान अधिकार बढ़ाए।

गलत विकल्प क्यों असफल हैं:
• विकल्प (a) में 1892 और 1909 का क्रम उलट है।
• विकल्प (b) में 1919 को 1909 से पहले रखा गया है।
• विकल्प (d) में पूरा क्रम उलट दिया गया है।

Value Addition:
• 1892 के अधिनियम को चुनाव 'सिद्धांत में' पेश करने वाला बताया गया है, बिना शब्द का प्रयोग किए।

• 1918 का Montagu-Chelmsford रिपोर्ट सीधे 1919 के अधिनियम से पहले आया।

en.display_text:
A historian documenting colonial-era elections records that, for the first time, a Muslim voter in a provincial constituency cast a direct ballot in an electorate exclusively constituted of Muslim voters, choosing a representative who would sit in the provincial legislative council. This electoral mechanism reflects which of the following legislative enactments?

(a) Indian Councils Act 1892
(b) Indian Councils Act 1909
(c) Government of India Act 1919
(d) Government of India Act 1935
en.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because students aware that the 1919 Act expanded communal electorates to Sikhs and Anglo-Indians may attribute the original introduction of separate electorates to the wrong Act.
elimination_logic: The scenario involves a Muslim voter in a legislative council election casting a ballot in a specially constituted Muslim electorate — this is the separate electorate system.
Separate electorates for Muslims were introduced for the first time under the Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms).
The 1919 Act continued and expanded this to other communities (Sikhs, Christians, Anglo-Indians) but did not introduce it.
The 1892 Act used indirect nomination — no direct voting by any community — eliminating option (a); option (b) correctly identifies 1909 as the origin.
en.final_explanation:
The Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) introduced two landmark but interlinked changes: direct elections for the first time and separate communal electorates for Muslims.

Applying the principle to the scenario: A Muslim voter exercising direct franchise in a constituency reserved exclusively for Muslim voters describes the separate electorate system introduced by the 1909 Act. Under this system, only Muslim voters could vote for Muslim seats, and only their representatives stood in those constituencies.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Indian Councils Act 1892 introduced indirect nomination through bodies like universities and chambers of commerce. Direct voting by individual members of a community was not a feature.
• Option (b) — Correct: The 1909 Act introduced both direct elections and separate Muslim electorates — precisely what the scenario describes.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Government of India Act 1919 extended communal representation to Sikhs, Christians, and Anglo-Indians, but the Muslim separate electorate originated in 1909.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Government of India Act 1935 continued and expanded communal representation but was not its origin.

Value Addition:
• Lord Minto accepted the Simla Deputation of Muslim leaders (1906) as the political basis for separate electorates.
• Morley explicitly stated he did not intend separate electorates to lead to parliamentary government — an ironic precursor to Partition.
• The Poona Pact (1932) replaced separate electorates for Scheduled Castes with reserved seats within joint electorates.

एक इतिहासकार जो औपनिवेशिक काल के चुनावों का दस्तावेजीकरण कर रहा है, उसने पहली बार यह रिकॉर्ड किया कि एक मुस्लिम मतदाता ने एक प्रांतीय निर्वाचन क्षेत्र में प्रत्यक्ष मतदान किया, जो केवल मुस्लिम मतदाताओं से गठित था, और एक ऐसा प्रतिनिधि चुना जो प्रांतीय विधान परिषद में बैठेगा। यह चुनावी तंत्र निम्नलिखित में से किस विधायी अधिनियम को दर्शाता है?

(a) भारतीय परिषद अधिनियम 1892
(b) भारतीय परिषद अधिनियम 1909
(c) भारत सरकार अधिनियम 1919
(d) भारत सरकार अधिनियम 1935
hi.strong_distractor: c — विकल्प c भ्रामक है क्योंकि छात्र जो जानते हैं कि 1919 का अधिनियम सिखों और एंग्लो-इंडियनों के लिए सामुदायिक मतदाता मंडलों का विस्तार करता है, वे अलग मतदाता मंडलों की मूल शुरुआत को गलत अधिनियम से जोड़ सकते हैं।
elimination_logic: यह परिदृश्य एक मुस्लिम मतदाता के विधान परिषद चुनाव में विशेष रूप से गठित मुस्लिम मतदाता मंडल में मतदान करने से संबंधित है — यह अलग मतदाता मंडल प्रणाली है।
मुसलमानों के लिए अलग मतदाता मंडल पहली बार भारतीय परिषद अधिनियम 1909 (मॉर्ले-मिंटो सुधार) के तहत लागू किए गए थे।
1919 का अधिनियम इसे अन्य समुदायों (सिख, ईसाई, एंग्लो-इंडियन) तक बढ़ाता है लेकिन इसकी शुरुआत नहीं करता।
1892 का अधिनियम अप्रत्यक्ष नामांकन का उपयोग करता था — किसी भी समुदाय द्वारा प्रत्यक्ष मतदान नहीं था — अतः विकल्प (a) खारिज; विकल्प (b) सही रूप से 1909 को मूल बताता है।
hi.final_explanation:
भारतीय परिषद अधिनियम 1909 (मॉर्ले-मिंटो सुधार) ने दो महत्वपूर्ण लेकिन परस्पर जुड़े बदलाव किए: पहली बार प्रत्यक्ष चुनाव और मुसलमानों के लिए अलग सामुदायिक मतदाता मंडल।

परिदृश्य पर लागू करते हुए: एक मुस्लिम मतदाता जो केवल मुस्लिम मतदाताओं के लिए आरक्षित निर्वाचन क्षेत्र में प्रत्यक्ष मताधिकार का प्रयोग करता है, वह 1909 के अधिनियम द्वारा प्रस्तुत अलग मतदाता मंडल प्रणाली को दर्शाता है। इस प्रणाली के तहत केवल मुस्लिम मतदाता ही मुस्लिम सीटों के लिए मतदान कर सकते थे, और केवल उनके प्रतिनिधि उन निर्वाचन क्षेत्रों में खड़े होते थे।

• विकल्प (a) — गलत: भारतीय परिषद अधिनियम 1892 ने विश्वविद्यालयों और वाणिज्य मंडलों जैसे निकायों के माध्यम से अप्रत्यक्ष नामांकन शुरू किया था। किसी समुदाय के व्यक्तिगत सदस्यों द्वारा प्रत्यक्ष मतदान इसकी विशेषता नहीं थी।
• विकल्प (b) — सही: 1909 का अधिनियम प्रत्यक्ष चुनाव और अलग मुस्लिम मतदाता मंडल दोनों को लागू करता है — बिल्कुल वैसा ही जैसा परिदृश्य में वर्णित है।
• विकल्प (c) — गलत: भारत सरकार अधिनियम 1919 ने सामुदायिक प्रतिनिधित्व को सिखों, ईसाइयों और एंग्लो-इंडियनों तक बढ़ाया, लेकिन मुस्लिम अलग मतदाता मंडल 1909 में शुरू हुआ था।
• विकल्प (d) — गलत: भारत सरकार अधिनियम 1935 ने सामुदायिक प्रतिनिधित्व को जारी रखा और बढ़ाया, लेकिन इसकी शुरुआत नहीं की।

• लॉर्ड मिंटो ने मुस्लिम नेताओं की शिमला डिप्यूटेशन (1906) को अलग मतदाता मंडलों के लिए राजनीतिक आधार के रूप में स्वीकार किया।
• मॉर्ले ने स्पष्ट रूप से कहा कि उनका उद्देश्य अलग मतदाता मंडल से संसदीय सरकार की स्थापना नहीं था — जो विभाजन का विडंबनापूर्ण पूर्वसूचक था।
• पूना समझौता (1932) ने अनुसूचित जातियों के लिए अलग मतदाता मंडलों को संयुक्त मतदाता मंडलों में आरक्षित सीटों से बदल दिया।

en.display_text:
Consider the following statements about financial provisions under the Government of India Act 1919:

Statement 1: This Act separated Central and Provincial finances for the first time, assigning specific revenue heads to each level of government.
Statement 2: Under this Act, provincial governments had complete financial autonomy and could raise any tax they deemed necessary without Central approval.

Which one of the following is correct?

(a) Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct
(b) Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are incorrect
(c) Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect
(d) Statement 1 is incorrect but Statement 2 is correct

statement_analysis.statement: The Government of India Act 1919 separated Central and Provincial finances for the first time, assigning specific revenue heads to each level.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1919 Act achieved the first formal separation of Central and Provincial finances, assigning certain revenue heads to provinces and others to the Centre — a foundational step toward fiscal federalism.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the 1919 Act, provincial governments had complete financial autonomy and could raise any tax they deemed necessary without Central approval.
statement_analysis.reason: Provincial financial autonomy under the 1919 Act was limited; the Centre retained authority over major revenue sources and provincial governments could not impose taxes freely — true financial autonomy came only with the 1935 Act's more detailed distribution.

en.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because Statement 1 is correct and students may assume Statement 2, which uses the language of 'autonomy' from the same Act, is also broadly correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The 1919 Act is explicitly recognised as the first formal separation of Central and Provincial finances — Statement 1 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: 'Complete financial autonomy' and 'any tax without Central approval' are extreme claims — provincial finances under 1919 remained constrained; the 1935 Act provided deeper separation — Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (c).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 uses the words 'complete' and 'without Central approval' to overstate what the 1919 Act actually granted. Students who correctly associate the 1919 Act with financial separation may read Statement 2 as a reasonable description of that separation, missing the qualifier 'complete' which makes it categorically false.
en.final_explanation:
The Government of India Act 1919 was a fiscal landmark in British India because it created the first formal boundary between Central and Provincial finances.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 1919 Act divided revenue heads for the first time, with certain taxes assigned to the Centre and others to provinces. This was essential for dyarchy to function — transferred departments needed identifiable revenue streams.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The scope of provincial financial autonomy was narrow. Provinces could not freely impose taxes; major revenue sources (customs, income tax) remained with the Centre. The Government of India Act 1935 introduced a far more detailed and generous distribution of financial powers.

Value Addition:
• The budget was divided into 'votable' and 'non-votable' grants under the 1919 Act — the Governor-General could certify rejected money bills.
• Full financial federalism in India was achieved through Articles 268–293 of the Constitution, which drew conceptually from the 1935 Act's revenue-sharing provisions.
• The Finance Commission under Article 280 of the Indian Constitution has its conceptual roots in the 1935 Act's federal grants-in-aid provisions, not the 1919 Act.

Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?

(a) Government of India Act 1919 — Introduced dyarchy at the Centre while provinces retained full autonomy
(b) Government of India Act 1935 — Introduced dyarchy in provinces while abolishing responsible government at the Centre
(c) Government of India Act 1919 — Introduced bicameral legislature in provinces for the first time
(d) Government of India Act 1935 — Introduced dyarchy at the Centre while abolishing provincial dyarchy and installing responsible government in provinces
en.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because students who know dyarchy was introduced in 1919 and continued in some form in 1935 may apply it to provinces, where it was actually abolished.
elimination_logic: Recall: The 1919 Act introduced dyarchy in provinces. The 1935 Act abolished provincial dyarchy and replaced it with full provincial autonomy.
The 1935 Act, however, introduced dyarchy at the Centre (Federal level) — Reserved and Transferred subjects at the Centre — which was never actually implemented.
Pair (d) states '1935 Act — Introduced dyarchy at the Centre while abolishing it in provinces' — this is the only correctly matched pair.
All other options either reverse the level at which dyarchy operated or attribute it to the wrong Act.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges the dyarchy of 1919 (provincial) with the dyarchy of 1935 (central). Students who associate 'dyarchy' with the 1919 Act may assume the 1935 Act simply continued or extended it, missing the critical reversal: the 1935 Act abolished dyarchy at the provincial level while simultaneously introducing it (on paper) at the central/federal level.
en.final_explanation:
Dyarchy — the division of governance into Reserved and Transferred subjects — was a defining feature of the 1919 Act at the provincial level. The 1935 Act made a structural inversion.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The 1919 Act introduced dyarchy in provinces, not the Centre; there was no central dyarchy under 1919.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The 1935 Act did not introduce dyarchy in provinces — it abolished it, replacing it with full responsible government at the provincial level.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Bicameralism at the Centre was introduced by the 1919 Act (Council of State + Legislative Assembly), not the 1935 Act.
• Option (d) — Correct: The 1935 Act introduced dyarchy at the Centre (Federal Reserved and Transferred subjects under the Governor-General) while simultaneously abolishing provincial dyarchy and installing responsible government in provinces.

Value Addition:
• Central dyarchy under 1935 was never operationalised because the All-India Federation itself never came into being.
• Provincial autonomy under 1935 was implemented from 1937; Congress ministries took office in seven provinces.
• Governor's special responsibilities and discretionary powers remained as significant 'safeguards' even under provincial autonomy.

en.display_text:
With reference to the Indian Independence Act 1947, consider the following statements:

1. British paramountcy over Princely States would lapse on the appointed day, leaving them legally free to join either dominion or remain independent.
2. The Act required that Princely States sign the Instrument of Accession before the appointed day, failing which they would automatically merge with the geographically contiguous dominion.
3. The Constituent Assemblies of both India and Pakistan were empowered by this Act to function as sovereign legislative bodies with the authority to repeal or amend the Act itself.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

(a) 1 and 3 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 1 and 2 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Independence Act 1947 provided that British paramountcy over Princely States would lapse on the appointed day, leaving them free to join either dominion or remain independent.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act explicitly terminated British paramountcy, leaving Princely States technically free — this created the integration challenge that Sardar Patel resolved through the Instrument of Accession.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Independence Act 1947 required that Princely States sign the Instrument of Accession before the appointed day, failing which they would automatically merge with whichever dominion they were geographically contiguous to.
statement_analysis.reason: The Act imposed no such automatic merger; it only lapsed paramountcy, leaving states free. The compulsion to accede came through political and administrative pressure by Sardar Patel and V.P. Menon, not through any legal mandate in the Act itself.

statement_analysis.statement: The Constituent Assemblies of both India and Pakistan were empowered under the 1947 Act to function as sovereign legislative bodies and could repeal or amend the Act itself.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1947 Act gave both Constituent Assemblies full legislative sovereignty — including the power to repeal the Indian Independence Act itself — making them supreme within their respective dominions.

en.strong_distractor: c — Option c (1 and 3 only) is the correct answer, but option (d) (all three) attracts students who do not examine Statement 2 carefully enough, assuming the Act logically must have specified an accession mechanism.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Lapse of paramountcy on the appointed day, leaving states free — this is textbook content; Statement 1 is Correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The Act imposed no automatic merger requirement; states were legally free post-paramountcy lapse — the integration was achieved through political means, not statutory mandate; Statement 2 is Incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Both Constituent Assemblies received full legislative sovereignty including the power to amend the 1947 Act — this is correct; Statement 3 is Correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct; option (a).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a partial-truth trap: it correctly identifies the Instrument of Accession as the mechanism through which states joined India, and it correctly notes the geographical contiguity consideration that Sardar Patel used as moral pressure. However, the Act itself contained no legal compulsion — the automatic merger clause is a fabrication. Students conflating Patel's political strategy with the statutory text will incorrectly validate Statement 2.
en.final_explanation:
The Indian Independence Act 1947 (passed by the British Parliament on 18 July 1947) was the legal instrument that terminated British sovereignty over India and Pakistan.

• Statement 1 — Correct: British paramountcy, which had given the Crown suzerainty over Princely States through treaties, lapsed entirely. States were theoretically free — creating the integration crisis that Sardar Patel resolved.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Act created no automatic merger or legal compulsion. Princely State integration was achieved through Sardar Patel's statecraft and the Instrument of Accession — a separate legal document — not through any clause in the Independence Act.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Act conferred complete legislative sovereignty on both Constituent Assemblies, explicitly including the power to abrogate the Independence Act itself — a dramatic transfer of parliamentary supremacy.

Value Addition:
• The Government of India Act 1935 continued as the interim constitution of both dominions until their own constitutions came into force.
• India's Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950; Pakistan's on 23 March 1956.
• Lord Mountbatten became Governor-General of India (not Pakistan) after independence — Jinnah became Pakistan's first Governor-General.

en.display_text:
With reference to the evolution of the judicial system in British India, consider the following statements:

1. The High Courts Act 1861 replaced both the Supreme Courts and the Sadar Courts, merging their jurisdictions into newly established High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.
2. The Federal Court established under the Government of India Act 1935 exercised original jurisdiction in centre-province disputes and appellate jurisdiction from High Courts on constitutional matters.
3. The Privy Council in London ceased to be the final court of appeal for India immediately upon the establishment of the Federal Court in 1935.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

(a) 1 only
(b) 3 only
(c) 1 and 2 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3

statement_analysis.statement: The High Courts Act 1861 replaced both the Supreme Courts (at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras) and the Sadar Courts, merging their jurisdictions into the newly established High Courts.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1861 Act amalgamated the Royal Charter Supreme Courts and the Company's Sadar Diwani Adalats and Sadar Nizamat Adalats into High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.

statement_analysis.statement: The Federal Court established under the Government of India Act 1935 could hear appeals from High Courts on constitutional matters and also exercised original jurisdiction in disputes between the Federation and Provinces.
statement_analysis.reason: The Federal Court had both original jurisdiction (inter-governmental disputes) and appellate jurisdiction (from High Courts on constitutional matters), making it structurally similar to the later Supreme Court of India.

statement_analysis.statement: The Privy Council in London ceased to be the final court of appeal for India immediately upon the establishment of the Federal Court in 1935.
statement_analysis.reason: The Privy Council continued as the final appellate authority even after the Federal Court was established in 1937; it was abolished as India's final court of appeal only by the Federal Court (Enlargement of Jurisdiction) Act 1947 and finally by the Constitution of India in 1950.

en.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three) is deceptive because Statements 1 and 2 are correct and the incorrect element in Statement 3 (about the Privy Council ceasing immediately) requires precise knowledge that many students lack.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: High Courts Act 1861 merged Supreme Courts and Sadar Courts — this is standard constitutional history; Statement 1 is Correct.
Statement 2: Federal Court's dual jurisdiction (original + appellate) is a standard feature; Statement 2 is Correct.
Statement 3: The Privy Council did NOT cease operations upon the 1935 Federal Court's establishment — it continued until 1949-50; Statement 3 is Incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, pointing to option (c).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap in Statement 3 replaces 'continued until 1950' with 'ceased immediately in 1935,' exploiting the intuitive but wrong assumption that establishing the Federal Court must have displaced the Privy Council. In reality, these two bodies co-existed for over a decade, with appeals going from High Courts → Federal Court → Privy Council on some matters.
en.final_explanation:
The evolution of India's higher judiciary spans nearly 200 years of colonial legislation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Indian High Courts Act 1861 established High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras by merging the Royal Charter Supreme Courts (created for British subjects) and the Company's Sadar Courts (for Indian subjects) — ending the dual judicial structure that had caused jurisdictional confusion.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Federal Court (est. 1937 under the 1935 Act) exercised original jurisdiction in centre-province disputes and appellate jurisdiction from High Courts on constitutional matters — making it a genuine constitutional court and direct ancestor of the Supreme Court.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Privy Council in London remained the ultimate court of appeal from India even after the Federal Court was established. It was only after the Federal Court (Enlargement of Jurisdiction) Act 1947 that the Privy Council's role diminished, and it was finally abolished as India's final appellate court when the Supreme Court came into being in 1950.

Value Addition:
• The Federal Court sat from 1937 to 1950, with Sir Maurice Gwyer as its first Chief Justice.
• The Supreme Court of India inherited the Federal Court's original jurisdiction and expanded it significantly.
• H.J. Kania became the first Chief Justice of India when the Supreme Court replaced the Federal Court in 1950.

en.display_text:
Which of the following is the correct chronological sequence in the evolution of communal representation in Indian legislative institutions?

1. Separate electorates extended to Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, and Indian Christians
2. Separate electorates for Muslims introduced for the first time
3. Separate electorates for depressed classes replaced by reserved seats in joint electorates
4. Abolition of all forms of separate electorates in the constitutional framework

(a) 2 → 3 → 1 → 4
(b) 2 → 1 → 3 → 4
(c) 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
(d) 2 → 1 → 4 → 3
en.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because students may confuse the sequence of the Communal Award (August 1932) and the Poona Pact (September 1932), or place the 1919 extension before the 1909 introduction.
elimination_logic: Anchor: Separate electorates for Muslims were introduced first, under the 1909 Act — this must come earliest.
The 1919 Act extended communal representation to Sikhs, Christians, and Anglo-Indians — second.
The Communal Award (August 1932) extended separate electorates to depressed classes; the Poona Pact (September 1932) replaced these with reserved seats in joint electorates — third, after 1919.
The Indian Constitution (1950) abolished separate electorates entirely — final step; option (b) is correct: 1909 → 1919 → Poona Pact 1932 → Constitution 1950.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap targets students who may place the Poona Pact before the 1919 extension, or who may confuse the Communal Award (1932) with the Poona Pact (1932). Both occurred in 1932 — the Award in August and the Pact in September — and their specific sequencing relative to each other is a frequent examination target. The question tests the broader arc: introduction → expansion → modification → abolition.
en.final_explanation:
The communal representation saga spans four decades of Indian constitutional history.

Correct sequence: 1909 → 1919 → Poona Pact 1932 → Indian Constitution 1950

• 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms): Separate electorates for Muslims introduced for the first time — Muslim voters could only vote for Muslim candidates in reserved Muslim seats.
• 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms): Communal representation expanded to Sikhs, Anglo-Indians, and Indian Christians — the principle became entrenched in multiple communities.
• Poona Pact 1932: Mahatma Gandhi's fast against the Communal Award (which gave Scheduled Castes separate electorates) compelled B.R. Ambedkar to accept reserved seats within joint electorates instead — a crucial modification.
• Indian Constitution 1950: Abolished separate electorates entirely, adopting reserved constituencies (reserved seats in joint electorates) as a substitute — reflecting the rejection of communalism while acknowledging social inequity.

Why wrong options fail:
• Any option placing 1919 before 1909 is wrong — the Muslim separate electorate predates the Sikh/Anglo-Indian extension.
• Placing the Poona Pact before the 1919 Act is chronologically impossible.

Value Addition:
• The Communal Award was announced by British PM Ramsay MacDonald on 16 August 1932.
• The Poona Pact was signed on 24 September 1932 between Gandhi and Ambedkar.
• Article 332 of the Constitution provides for reservation of seats for SCs and STs in State Legislatures — distinct from separate electorates.

सांप्रदायिक प्रतिनिधित्व की कहानी भारतीय संवैधानिक इतिहास के चार दशकों को समेटे हुए है।

सही क्रम: 1909 → 1919 → पूना समझौता 1932 → भारतीय संविधान 1950

• 1909 (मॉर्ले-मिंटो सुधार): मुसलमानों के लिए पहली बार पृथक निर्वाचन क्षेत्र लागू किए गए — मुस्लिम मतदाता केवल मुस्लिम उम्मीदवारों के लिए आरक्षित मुस्लिम सीटों पर मतदान कर सकते थे।
• 1919 (मोंटैगु-चेल्म्सफोर्ड सुधार): सांप्रदायिक प्रतिनिधित्व सिखों, एंग्लो-इंडियनों और भारतीय ईसाइयों तक विस्तारित हुआ — यह सिद्धांत कई समुदायों में स्थापित हो गया।
• पूना समझौता 1932: महात्मा गांधी के सांप्रदायिक पुरस्कार (जिसने अनुसूचित जातियों को पृथक निर्वाचन क्षेत्र दिए थे) के खिलाफ उपवास ने बी.आर. अम्बेडकर को संयुक्त निर्वाचन क्षेत्रों में आरक्षित सीटें स्वीकार करने के लिए मजबूर किया — एक महत्वपूर्ण संशोधन।
• भारतीय संविधान 1950: पृथक निर्वाचन क्षेत्रों को पूरी तरह समाप्त कर दिया, और आरक्षित निर्वाचन क्षेत्रों (संयुक्त निर्वाचन क्षेत्रों में आरक्षित सीटें) को विकल्प के रूप में अपनाया — सांप्रदायिकता को अस्वीकार करते हुए सामाजिक असमानता को स्वीकार करते हुए।

en.display_text:
With reference to the financial provisions of the Government of India Act 1935, consider the following:

Assertion (a): The Government of India Act 1935 introduced federal grants-in-aid provisions to assist provinces with limited revenue capacity, creating a mechanism for vertical fiscal transfer between the federation and the provinces.

Reason (R): The Finance Commission of India, established under Article 280 of the Constitution, is conceptually descended from these federal grants-in-aid provisions of the 1935 Act, which served as the prototype for independent India's fiscal federalism architecture.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above?

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect
(d) A is incorrect but R is correct
en.strong_distractor: b — Option b is deceptive because students may recognise both A and R as correct but doubt whether the federal grants provisions of 1935 are directly ancestral to the Finance Commission concept.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (a) correct? The Government of India Act 1935 introduced federal grants-in-aid provisions to assist provinces — this is verified; A is correct.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? The Finance Commission under Article 280 of the Indian Constitution performs a devolution and grants function conceptually rooted in the 1935 Act's federal financial provisions — this is accepted constitutional history; R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? R explains why the 1935 Act's grants provisions are historically significant — they were the conceptual model from which the Finance Commission mechanism evolved. R directly establishes the importance and lineage of what A describes — R does explain A.
Both A and R correct, R explains A — correct option is (a).
en.final_explanation:
The Government of India Act 1935 introduced the most detailed fiscal federal framework in India's colonial history, dividing taxing powers between the federation and provinces and creating federal grants-in-aid provisions.

Assertion (a): The 1935 Act included provisions for federal grants-in-aid to provinces — particularly for provinces with limited revenue potential — creating a mechanism for vertical fiscal transfer. This is factually correct.

Reason (R): The Finance Commission under Article 280 of the Indian Constitution, which recommends the devolution of Central tax revenues to States and grants-in-aid, is conceptually descended from these 1935 provisions. Constitutional historians trace the Finance Commission's mandate directly to this colonial precedent. R is also factually correct.

Causal Link: R explains A because it identifies precisely why the 1935 Act's grant provisions matter constitutionally — they were not merely administrative details but the prototype for independent India's fiscal federalism mechanism. R gives A its significance.

Value Addition:
• The First Finance Commission of India was constituted in 1951 under N.R. Sarkar.
• Articles 268–293 of the Indian Constitution govern financial relations between the Union and States.
• The 1935 Act assigned income tax, customs, and excise duties to the federation — a distribution framework closely mirrored in the current constitutional scheme.

With reference to the franchise and electoral provisions of the Government of India Act 1935, consider the following statements:

1. This Act extended franchise on the basis of property and educational qualifications, but the electorate remained limited to approximately 10–12 percent of the total population.
2. The Act abolished all forms of communal and separate electorates, replacing them with a unified territorial electorate for all communities.
3. The Act provided special representation for women, labour interests, commerce and industry, and universities — beyond the standard communal and territorial electorates.

Which of the above statements is/are NOT correct?

(a) 1 only
(b) 2 only
(c) 1 and 3 only
(d) 2 and 3 only

statement_analysis.statement: The Government of India Act 1935 extended franchise on the basis of property and educational qualifications, but the electorate remained limited to approximately 10–12 percent of the total population.
statement_analysis.reason: Despite being a significant expansion from 1919, the 1935 franchise covered only about 10–12% of India's population — far from universal suffrage.

statement_analysis.statement: The 1935 Act abolished all forms of communal and separate electorates, replacing them with a unified territorial electorate for all communities.
statement_analysis.reason: The 1935 Act continued and expanded communal electorates — it did not abolish them. Separate electorates for Muslims, Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans were all preserved and, in some cases, extended.

statement_analysis.statement: The 1935 Act provided special representation for women, labour interests, commerce and industry, and universities — beyond the standard communal and territorial electorates.
statement_analysis.reason: Special seats for these functional constituencies were part of the 1935 Act's electoral architecture, reflecting an attempt at functional representation.

en.strong_distractor: c — Option c (1 and 3 only) is deceptive because Statements 1 and 3 are both correct, and students may select this thinking the question asks for correct statements, missing the 'NOT correct' qualifier.
elimination_logic: Read the stem: asks which statement is NOT correct.
Statement 1: 10–12% franchise with property/educational qualifications — a well-known fact about 1935; this is Correct.
Statement 2: Claims 1935 abolished communal electorates — the opposite is true; the 1935 Act continued and expanded them; Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Statement 3: Special seats for women, labour, commerce, universities — confirmed feature of 1935; this is Correct.
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — option (b).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the scope-extension trap by claiming 'abolished all forms of communal and separate electorates' — a claim that is factually the opposite of what the 1935 Act did. Students who associate 'abolition of separate electorates' with the Indian Constitution (1950) may erroneously attribute this to the 1935 Act, particularly if they confuse the Poona Pact's modification of Scheduled Caste electorates with a general abolition.
en.final_explanation:
The Government of India Act 1935 expanded the electorate significantly from 1919 but fell far short of universal suffrage and retained the communal representation framework.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The electorate expanded to about 30 million voters (10–12% of population), up from about 6.5 million under 1919. Property and literacy qualifications determined eligibility.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This is the NOT correct statement. The 1935 Act retained and expanded communal electorates for Muslims, Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans. Separate electorates were not abolished until the Indian Constitution came into force in 1950.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Act created special seats for women, labour, commerce and industry, and universities — functional representation alongside territorial and communal categories.

Value Addition:
• The 1935 elections (held 1937) saw Congress win majorities in seven of eleven provinces.
• Universal adult franchise was adopted by the Indian Constitution — Article 326 — eliminating property/educational qualifications.
• The 1935 Act's continuation of communal electorates was one of Congress's major objections to the Act.

en.display_text:
With reference to the Indian Councils Act 1892, consider the following:

Assertion (a): The Act enhanced the powers of Legislative Councils by allowing members to discuss the budget and address questions to the executive, though voting on financial matters was not permitted.

Reason (R): The Act deliberately avoided the term 'election,' instead using the mechanism of 'recommendation' through bodies such as universities, district boards, and chambers of commerce, from which the Governor-General then nominated members.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above?

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect
(d) A is incorrect but R is correct
en.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because students who correctly identify that the 1892 Act avoided the term 'election' may assume Reason R (about the term 'election') is incorrect, leading them to option (c).
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (a) correct? The Indian Councils Act 1892 allowed Legislative Council members to discuss (but not vote on) the budget and to question the executive — Yes; A is correct.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? The 1892 Act did not use the term 'election' — it used 'recommendation' through bodies like universities and chambers of commerce, avoiding the formal term while introducing the principle — Yes; R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? The avoidance of the word 'election' explains the political caution of British authorities — they expanded legislative functions (discussion, questioning) incrementally while avoiding a full electoral mandate. R explains the cautious expansion in A by showing the deliberate political restraint built into the Act.
Both A and R correct, R explains A — correct option is (a).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap works subtly here. Students may read R as a statement about terminology and assume it has no causal relationship to A (which is about legislative powers). In fact, R explains A: the British deliberately limited both the electoral mandate (avoiding the word 'election') and legislative powers (discussion without voting) as part of the same cautious strategy of incremental reform. The two features — limited nomination and limited powers — were conceptually linked as deliberate half-measures.
en.final_explanation:
The Indian Councils Act 1892 is best understood as a carefully calibrated half-step: it introduced electoral-like procedures and expanded legislative functions without committing to genuine representative government.

Assertion (a): The Act allowed Legislative Council members to discuss the budget and submit questions to the executive — a significant enhancement over the 1861 Act, which had no such provisions. This is factually correct.

Reason (R): The Act conspicuously avoided the word 'election,' using instead the language of 'recommendation' and 'nomination upon recommendation' — bodies like universities, district boards, and chambers of commerce recommended names that the executive then formally nominated. This avoidance was deliberate. R is factually correct.

Causal Link: R explains A because both features — the avoidance of the electoral term and the restriction of powers to discussion rather than voting — reflect the same colonial strategy of managed, limited reform. Expanding powers slightly while withholding democratic legitimacy was the consistent approach of the 1892 Act.

Value Addition:
• The 1892 Act is called the 'first step toward representative institutions' but fell far short of responsible government.
• The budget could be discussed but not voted on — a critical distinction from real parliamentary control.
• Gopal Krishna Gokhale used the budget discussion provisions skillfully to criticise colonial expenditure.

(a) Creation of the Secretary of State for India, assisted by a Council of India
(b) Introduction of a bicameral central legislature comprising a Council of State and a Legislative Assembly
(c) Governor-General assuming the additional title of Viceroy to represent the Crown directly
(d) Simultaneous abolition of the Court of Directors and the Board of Control
en.strong_distractor: a — Option a (Secretary of State for India) is deceptive because students know the Secretary of State was a powerful figure throughout colonial India and may assume his role was first created in 1919.

Option (b) — 'Introduction of bicameral legislature at the Centre with Council of State and Legislative Assembly' — is a feature of the 1919 Act, not the 1858 Act.

en.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges features of the 1858 and 1919 Acts. In fact, the 1858 Act was about Crown-Company transition — it created the Secretary of State, abolished the Board of Control and Court of Directors, and made the Governor-General a Viceroy. en.final_explanation:
The Government of India Act 1858 was about administrative restructuring — transferring power from Company to Crown. It had nothing to do with legislative structure at the centre.

• Option (a) — Creation of Secretary of State for India: A 1858 Act feature. The Secretary of State, a Cabinet minister, replaced the Board of Control and assumed superintendence over Indian affairs.
• Option (b) — Bicameral legislature with Council of State and Legislative Assembly: This is a 1919 Act feature. It does NOT belong to the 1858 Act — this is the odd one out.
• Option (c) — Governor-General assuming the additional title of Viceroy: A 1858 Act feature. The Viceroy represented the Crown directly; Lord Canning was the first.
• Option (d) — Abolition of the Court of Directors and Board of Control: A 1858 Act feature. Both Company governing bodies were dissolved, ending the Company era.

Value Addition:
• The 1858 Act transferred power but changed little about day-to-day administration on the ground.

en.display_text:
A constitutional historian notes: 'Following the announcement of a British award granting separate electorates to depressed class communities, a political agreement was reached between two Indian leaders under which these separate electorates were abandoned in exchange for an increased number of reserved seats within joint electorates — a compromise that shaped the subsequent constitutional framework for political representation of marginalised communities.'

The political agreement described above refers to which of the following?

(a) The Communal Award of 1932
(b) The Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909
(c) The Poona Pact of 1932
(d) The Government of India Act 1935
en.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because students who know the Communal Award involved depressed classes may incorrectly attribute the resolution to the same instrument rather than the separate Poona Pact.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a situation where a political agreement replaced separate electorates for a group with reserved seats in joint electorates — this is the Poona Pact (September 1932).
The Communal Award (August 1932) initially granted separate electorates to depressed classes — it was the Poona Pact that reversed this specific provision.
Eliminate option (a): the Communal Award created the separate electorates for depressed classes; it did not resolve the controversy — it caused it.
Option (c) — the Poona Pact — is the agreement that replaced separate electorates for depressed classes with reserved seats in joint electorates.
en.final_explanation:
The Communal Award of August 1932, announced by British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, granted separate electorates to the Depressed Classes (Scheduled Castes) among others. Mahatma Gandhi, who was imprisoned at the time, began a fast unto death to protest this, arguing that separate electorates would permanently divide Hindu society.

Applying the principle: The scenario describes a political agreement that converted separate electorates into reserved seats within joint electorates — precisely what the Poona Pact (24 September 1932) achieved. B.R. Ambedkar negotiated with Gandhi and agreed to forgo separate electorates in exchange for a significantly increased number of reserved seats within general (joint) electorates.

• Option (a) — Communal Award: This is what created the separate electorates — it did not resolve the controversy; it triggered it.
• Option (b) — Morley-Minto Reforms (1909): These introduced separate electorates for Muslims, not Scheduled Castes, and had no mechanism for the type of resolution described.
• Option (c) — Poona Pact: Correctly describes the agreement where reserved seats replaced separate electorates for depressed classes.
• Option (d) — Government of India Act 1935: This Act retained communal representation but was a statutory framework, not a political agreement between leaders.

Value Addition:
• The number of reserved seats for depressed classes was increased from 71 (Communal Award) to 148 under the Poona Pact.
• The Poona Pact is seen as a major point of divergence in the Gandhi-Ambedkar relationship.
• The Indian Constitution (Article 330) provides for reserved constituencies for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha — the direct constitutional descendant of the Poona Pact model.

सिद्धांत लागू करते हुए: परिदृश्य एक राजनीतिक समझौते का वर्णन करता है जिसने अलग निर्वाचन मंडलों को संयुक्त निर्वाचन मंडलों में आरक्षित सीटों में बदल दिया — ठीक वही जो Poona Pact (24 सितंबर 1932) ने किया। बी.आर. अम्बेडकर ने गांधी के साथ बातचीत की और अलग निर्वाचन मंडलों को छोड़ने के बदले सामान्य (संयुक्त) निर्वाचन मंडलों में आरक्षित सीटों की संख्या में काफी वृद्धि पर सहमति दी।

• विकल्प (a) — Communal Award: इसने अलग निर्वाचन मंडल बनाए; विवाद का समाधान नहीं किया, बल्कि इसे जन्म दिया।
• विकल्प (b) — Morley-Minto सुधार (1909): इन सुधारों ने मुसलमानों के लिए अलग निर्वाचन मंडल बनाए, न कि अनुसूचित जातियों के लिए, और इस प्रकार के समाधान के लिए कोई व्यवस्था नहीं थी।
• विकल्प (c) — Poona Pact: सही विकल्प है जो बताता है कि आरक्षित सीटों ने depressed classes के लिए अलग निर्वाचन मंडलों की जगह ली।
• विकल्प (d) — Government of India Act 1935: इस अधिनियम ने सामुदायिक प्रतिनिधित्व बनाए रखा लेकिन यह एक वैधानिक ढांचा था, नेताओं के बीच राजनीतिक समझौता नहीं।

• Communal Award के तहत depressed classes के लिए आरक्षित सीटें 71 थीं, जो Poona Pact के तहत 148 हो गईं।
